n: In this lesson we study the further groups of functional poisons. The plan has six parts. First, ethyl alcohol: kinetics, diagnosis and post-mortem signs. Then alcohol surrogates: methanol, glycol and TEL. The third part is hypnotics, that is, barbiturates and tranquillisers. Then stimulant poisons: psychotonics and strychnine. The fifth part is mediator poisons: atropine, pilocarpine and clonidine. Finally we consider a practical case of methanol poisoning.

The first section: ethyl alcohol, in brief. Among deaths from poisoning, ethyl alcohol holds the leading place. The narcotic action is linked with inhibition of the cerebral cortex. The lethal dose is 250–300 ml. Gas chromatography is used as the quantitative method. The degree of intoxication is assessed by the blood per mille. In the body there is no characteristic sign, and no specific change is found. Remember these five points in the order of the table.

t: Mechanism of action of ethyl alcohol
n: The mechanism of action of ethyl alcohol. The lethal dose is 250–300 ml. The action proceeds in stages. First the cortex is inhibited. After that the subcortex is left uncontrolled and excitation appears. In most people inhibition spreads downwards. Finally the respiratory and cardiac centres are disturbed. That is, the earlier excitation is in fact a result of inhibition, and later the vital centres are damaged too.

Endogenous alcohol, that is, alcohol formed in the body itself. Usually its amount may reach 0.3–0.4 per mille. In strong mental stress, trauma, exposure to cold and physical exertion it decreases. With positive emotions, hypoxia, diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive bronchitis, and diseases of the central nervous system, liver and kidney, it increases. This means that in assessing the analytical result, the natural background must be taken into account.

Absorption and the resorption period. The resorption period is usually 1–2 hours. Alcohol is absorbed 20 % from the stomach and 80 % from the intestine. On an empty stomach about 5 % is bound and not absorbed. With a full stomach about 40 % is temporarily bound. Resorption is shortened with an empty stomach and hypoacid gastritis. With a full stomach and hyperacid gastritis it is lengthened. Thus the state of the stomach determines the rate of absorption.

Metabolism of ethyl alcohol. 90 % of alcohol is metabolised, and the rest is eliminated in urine and through the lungs. ADH is alcohol dehydrogenase and ALDH is aldehyde dehydrogenase; these are enzymes. The chain is as follows: ethyl alcohol is converted to acetaldehyde, with the enzyme ADH taking part. Then acetaldehyde passes to acetic acid, with the enzyme ALDH working. Finally water and carbon dioxide are formed. Remember the names of the enzymes and the order.

Acetaldehyde and atypical enzymes. With atypical enzymes death is also possible. Under the action of acetaldehyde, headache, weakness, nausea, vomiting, raised blood pressure and tachycardia are observed, and hallucinations are called a “hangover”. In atypical enzymes the activity of alcohol dehydrogenase is very high, while aldehyde dehydrogenase is deficient. As a result acetaldehyde accumulates quickly. For this reason, even with a small amount of alcohol, severe intoxication occurs.

Clinical signs. The clinical picture depends on dose, time and stomach contents. At first euphoria and psychomotor excitation are observed. Then drowsiness and disturbance of movement and speech appear. After that nausea and vomiting join. In some cases coma develops. That is, the signs change gradually from excitation to depression.

Alcohol-related death, that is, the concept of “alcohol related death”. Death from poisoning holds the leading place. In intoxication, diseases create a predisposition to non-violent death. In intoxication other deaths also occur: accident, suicide and homicide. According to WHO data, about 2.5 million cases have been recorded in recent years. In diagnosis, the presence and amount of alcohol are important.

t: Qualitative detection in a living person
n: Qualitative detection of alcohol in a living person. Here the exhaled air is examined. The Rappoport method dates from 1928: potassium permanganate and sulphuric acid are used, Mn(VII) passes to Mn(II) and the pinkish-red colour disappears. The Mokhov–Shinkarenko method dates from 1955: bichromate and sulphuric acid are used, Cr(VI) passes to Cr(III) and the yellow colour changes to green. In both methods, a change in the colour of the reagent indicates the presence of alcohol.

Performance of the Rappoport test. First test tubes are prepared with 2 ml of distilled water. Air is blown into the first tube for 20–30 seconds. Then the reagent is added: sulphuric acid and a drop of KMnO₄. Result: if the colour disappears, alcohol is present. Sensitivity begins at 0.3–0.4 per mille in the blood. A false positive result is possible in caries, diabetes and lung disease. Therefore approach the result with caution.

Rules for taking samples. Samples are taken as early as possible. From the body, peripheral venous blood and urine are taken. From a living person, samples are taken several times at intervals. Each sample volume is at least 5 ml. The container must be full, with no air. Storage is in a refrigerator, and the time is recorded. These rules are necessary for the result to be reliable.

The ratio of alcohol in blood and urine. This ratio gives an idea of the time of drinking. In the resorption period it is higher in the blood than in the urine and there is a rise in the blood. In the elimination period the concentration in the blood falls but remains high in the urine. On repeated intake, if it is high in the urine and rises again in the blood, it is assessed as renewed drinking. That is, the ratio shows at which stage the alcohol is in the body.

The Widmark constant β. If it is not possible, the average of 0.13–0.15 is taken. The values in the table are in per mille per hour. At the start of elimination 0.10–0.13. With moderate load 0.15–0.18. With heavy load 0.20–0.24. In sleep 0.10–0.12, in coma below 0.10. In chilling 0.20–0.25, in tolerance 0.3–0.4. So β changes according to the state.

The Widmark–Balyakin formula: A = R·r·(Ct + P·T). The meaning of the symbols. A is the amount of alcohol, in terms of 100°. R is body weight, kg. r is the reduction factor, 0.68 for a man and 0.55 for a woman. Ct is the concentration of alcohol in the blood. P · T is the constant multiplied by time, in hours. The formula is used to calculate the amount of alcohol drunk.

Degrees of intoxication. They are assessed by ethyl alcohol in the blood. 0.5–1.5 ‰ mild intoxication. 1.5–2.5 ‰ moderate intoxication. 2.5–3.0 ‰ severe intoxication. Above 3.0 ‰ poisoning. If in the body it is 5.0 ‰ or more, the cause of death is acute poisoning. However, with higher alcohols death may occur even below 4 per mille.

t: Examination of the body: ethyl alcohol
n: Examination of the body: ethyl alcohol. No specific morphological change is found. External signs: the face is bluish and puffy, subconjunctival ecchymoses. Internal signs: a specific odour from the cavities, congestion of the brain and organs, cerebral oedema, petechial haemorrhages. The urinary bladder is full. These signs are general in character, not only for alcohol.

The second section: alcohol surrogates, in brief. Surrogate in English means “substitute”. A surrogate is a drink that replaces ethyl alcohol. This includes methyl, propyl, butyl and amyl alcohol. There are also ethylene glycol, denatured alcohol and TEL. The most common is methyl alcohol, because its colour and odour are similar. Therefore it is difficult to distinguish it from ethyl alcohol.

Lethal doses of surrogates. For comparison: ethyl alcohol 250–300 ml. Methyl alcohol 30–100 ml. Propyl alcohol 300 ml. Butyl alcohol 200–250 ml. Amyl alcohol 20–30 ml. Ethylene glycol 100–200 ml. It can be seen that amyl and methyl alcohol are dangerous in a considerably smaller amount than ethyl alcohol.

Toxicokinetics of methanol. The metabolites are strongly toxic, and oxidation is slow. Methanol itself is a weak narcotic. From its transformation, formaldehyde and formic acid are formed. As a result acidosis develops and enzymes are weakened. Finally tissue respiration is disturbed. Thus the main danger comes not from methanol itself but from its metabolites.

Clinical stages of methanol. Decreased vision leads to complete blindness. The first stage is intoxication: weak, brief, then deep sleep. The second stage is latent: the condition improves, lasting from hours to a day. The third stage is the height: vomiting, abdominal pain, visual disturbance. The fourth stage is death: after 2–3 days, paralysis of the respiratory centre. Remember: the good condition in the latent period is deceptive.

Methanol: examination of the body. Forensic chemistry detects it for 3–5 days. The lividity and blood are reddish-grey, the blood is thickened. In the brain there is oedema, and in the brainstem focal haemorrhage. Under the epicardium there are plaque-like haemorrhages, that is, Kryukov spots. In the optic nerve there are haemorrhage, oedema and degeneration. In a prolonged course, degeneration of the heart, liver and kidney is added.

Higher alcohols. With them coma is observed, then paralysis of the respiratory centre. Brain changes are more marked than those in the heart. With propyl alcohol the lethal dose is 300 ml. With butyl alcohol the lethal dose is 200–250 ml, and a sweet odour comes from the internal organs. With amyl alcohol the lethal dose is 20–30 ml, and the odour of fusel oils is noticed. That is, the odour helps to suggest the substance.

Metabolism of ethylene glycol. This is antifreeze and brake fluid, usually an accident. Ethylene glycol is a dihydric alcohol. It is converted to glycolaldehyde. Then oxalic acid is formed. Finally oxalates are excreted in the urine. Remember this chain in order.

Ethylene glycol: four stages. The lethal dose is 100–200 ml. The first stage is intoxication: signs and a short latent period. The second stage is CNS damage: first excitation, then depression. The third stage is liver and kidney, with clinical signs from these organs. The fourth stage is death: the cause is cerebral coma or hepatorenal failure. Thus poisoning begins with intoxication and ends with organ failure.

t: Ethylene glycol: death and the body
n: Ethylene glycol: death and the body. Forensic chemistry detects it in blood and organs for 3–6 days. In the first days cerebral coma, congestion of organs, diffuse diapedetic haemorrhages, cerebral oedema and perivascular haemorrhages are observed. Later hepatorenal failure develops: toxic hepatitis, nephrosis, hydropic degeneration and necronephrosis. That is, with time one passes from brain changes to damage of the liver and kidney.

Tetraethyl lead, that is, TEL. The lethal dose is 10–15 ml, and it persists up to 3 months. Properties: oily, volatile, with an apple odour. It is added to low-octane petrol as an antiknock agent. Route of entry: by mouth, respiratory tract and the whole skin. In the clinical picture psychosis, hallucinations and coma are observed. In the body there is an apple odour, and neuronal degeneration is found.

The third section: hypnotics, in brief. Barbiturates increase vascular permeability. Poisoning is suicide or an accident. Groups: barbiturates, that is, luminal, veronal, barbamyl, medinal, nembutal and cyclobarbital. Piperidine derivative noxiron. Pyridine derivative tetridin. Tranquillisers: elenium, seduxen and meprobamate.

t: Hypnotics: clinical picture and lethal doses
n: The clinical picture and lethal doses of hypnotics. Barbamyl and nembutal 1.0–2.0 g. Medinal and tetridin 3.0–5.0, noxiron 5.0–10 g. The clinical picture develops in sequence. First deep sleep. Then blood pressure and temperature fall and breathing is disturbed. Then areflexia and coma. Finally death, from paralysis of the respiratory centre.

Hypnotics: factors raising the risk. Co-ingestion raises the risk of death. Even a small dose is dangerous in old age, in cardiovascular disease and in respiratory disease. The effect is intensified when taken in a state of intoxication, with alcoholic drink and together with other sedatives. This means that, along with the dose of the drug, the condition is also important.

Hypnotics: the body and diagnosis. Qualitative examination is not enough; quantitative is needed. The body shows signs of rapid death, with no characteristic change. Tablet remnants may be present in the stomach. The basis of diagnosis is the incident, clinical picture and forensic chemistry. Why is quantitative analysis needed? Because it may be a therapeutic dose. In the clinic the samples are blood, urine and gastric lavage fluid.

The fourth section: stimulant poisons, in brief. From the forensic standpoint strychnine and cicuta are important. Psychotonics: caffeine, phenamine, phenatine. Antidepressants: imizin, indopan, kuredal. Convulsant poisons: strychnine and cicuta. These three groups stimulate the central nervous system.

Psychotonics and antidepressants. With regular intake habituation develops. Psychotonics raise the tone of the higher parts of the CNS. In a large dose there are tremor and convulsions, tachycardia, raised blood pressure, delirium and psychosis with hallucinations. Antidepressants are MAO inhibitors. With them headache, vomiting, raised temperature and blood pressure, and disturbance of rhythm and consciousness occur.

Strychnine: source and action. It stimulates the respiratory and circulatory centres. Source: seeds of nux vomica and “rvotny koren” (vomiting root). Action: the spinal reflex is increased. In medicine it is used for digestion and metabolism. Elimination is slow, mainly through the kidney. Another use is as a rodent poison.

The clinical course of strychnine. An attack lasts several minutes, then relaxation follows. First muscle twitching and difficulty in swallowing. Then a tonic convulsive attack begins. Consciousness is preserved, and opisthotonus is observed. Light and sound provoke a new attack. Remember: during the convulsions the patient does not lose consciousness.

Strychnine: death, dose and the body. 0.1–0.3 g for adults, 0.005 g for small children. The time of death is several hours. In the body rigidity develops rapidly and strongly. Because strychnine is a stable poison, it is detected in the body for months. For this reason forensic chemistry is of decisive importance.

The fifth section: mediator poisons, in brief. These are poisons acting on mediators. Lethal doses: atropine sulphate 0.1 g for adults, pilocarpine 0.06 g, pachycarpine 1.0–2.0 g, clonidine 0.005–0.01 g for adults. For muscle relaxants no dose is given. Remember these figures from the table together with the name of the substance.

The course of atropine poisoning. Death occurs on the first day from the cardiac or respiratory centre. The signs in sequence: the face reddens, the mouth dries. The pupil dilates, vision is disturbed. Delirium and agitation appear. Swallowing becomes difficult, the pulse is rapid, and atony is observed.

We compare atropine and pilocarpine. Pilocarpine usually occurs when administered by mistake. With atropine the pupil dilates, the mouth and throat are dry, the face reddens, the pulse quickens, and there are delirium and psychic agitation. With pilocarpine, by contrast: the pupil constricts, much sweat and saliva are secreted, there are bronchospasm and pulmonary oedema, abdominal pain and diarrhoea. That is, they give opposite signs.

Pachycarpine and clonidine. Clonidine is dangerous in children even at 0.004 g. Pachycarpine is an n-cholinolytic and acts strongly on the uterus. It is used in attempts to terminate pregnancy. Vomiting, convulsions and collapse are observed, and death occurs in the first hours. Clonidine is an alpha-adrenoblocker. It is added to a drink. Blood pressure falls, and bradycardia, hypothermia and loss of consciousness are observed.

Poisoning with muscle relaxants. Forensic chemical results are important in diagnosis. Action: they block the nerve-muscle impulse. In surgery they are used in anaesthesia. Examples: listenon, tubarin, ditilin. The cause of poisoning is violation of the rules or hypersensitivity. The cause of death is paralysis of the respiratory muscles.

t: Teaching case: a liquid drunk instead of alcohol
n: Teaching case: a liquid drunk instead of alcohol. This is a hypothetical case, not a real examination. Given: a liquid was drunk instead of alcohol. Mild intoxication, then deep sleep. Then the condition was good for a time. Then vomiting and reduced vision. In the body, Kryukov spots. Questions: which surrogate is likely? Which stages were observed? For how many days does forensic chemistry detect it?

Case answer: methanol poisoning. The set of signs corresponds to methanol. The surrogate is methyl alcohol, that is, methanol. Stages: intoxication, latent, height. It is dangerous because formaldehyde and formic acid are formed. Plaque-like haemorrhages under the epicardium are Kryukov spots. Forensic chemistry detects it for 3–5 days.

Conclusion: main points of support. In functional poisons there is no marked morphological change. For ethyl alcohol the support is the blood per mille and gas chromatography. For methanol, the latent stage and visual disturbance. For ethylene glycol, hepatorenal damage and oxalate. For hypnotics, quantitative analysis and the circumstances of the incident. For strychnine, convulsions, opisthotonus and rapid rigidity.

The review questions rest on pp. 156–167 of the chapter. What are the metabolism and lethal dose of ethyl alcohol? What is the Rappoport test based on? What are the Widmark constant and the meaning of the formula? What are the stages and post-mortem signs in methanol poisoning? How are ethylene glycol and strychnine diagnosed? By answering these questions, consolidate the lesson.
